passages.title: The two oaths and the remaking of the bones
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Qiyāmah opens the way a solemn declaration opens: with an oath — in fact with two. Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul, and what He swears *to* is left unspoken because the whole sūrah is about to spell it out: that the Resurrection is real and will come to pass. Ayat 3 and 4 take up the objection the deniers keep repeating — how can bones reduced to dust be gathered again? — and answer it with more than it asked for. Ayat 5 and 6 then turn from the argument to the man making it, and expose two things: his real motive ("he wants to run on ahead") and his sneer ("so when is this Day?").

Two ayat of oath, two of objection and answer, two of exposure. That is the shape of the passage, and it holds together because all six are answering a single denial.

## The "lā" that is not a "no"

Both oaths begin with a word that stops readers short. Ayah 1 reads *lā uqsimu bi-yawmi'l-qiyāmah* — with the Arabic negative particle *lā*, "nay" or "not," attached to the verb "I swear." Ayah 2 repeats it: *wa-lā uqsimu bi'n-nafsi'l-lawwāmah*. Yet the translations in front of us render both as emphatic affirmations: "I do swear by the Day of Judgment!" Why?

Ibn Kathir notes that this point has been made before, more than once: when the thing being sworn about is something that is being **negated** — that is, when the oath is answering someone's denial — it is permissible to use the word *lā* before the oath to emphasise that negation. Here, he says, what is being sworn about is "the affirmation of the final abode and the refutation against the claim of the ignorant that the resurrection of bodies will not occur."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunter about the grammar: the negative particle prefixed to the oath in this context "has no meaning" of its own — it is not negating the oath. When the purpose of an oath is to refute an opponent's false thought, this redundant negative particle is placed in front of it. The commentary adds that the idiom is commonplace in Arabic, and that Urdu does the same thing when answering an objection, repudiating something already said, or emphasising an important subject.

So the *lā* is not aimed at the oath. It is aimed at the denial the sūrah has come to refute — the very claim the man in ayah 6 makes with his mocking question. It sweeps his claim off the table first, and only then does the oath land. Qatadah cut through the whole discussion with a simple gloss: "This means, I swear by both of these things" — reported likewise from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd bin Jubayr (Ibn Kathir).

**And notice what is missing.** An oath in Arabic normally has a complement — the statement it swears to. Here none is spoken. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it is understood from the context: *that the Day of Resurrection is a reality and it shall come to pass*. The silence is itself rhetoric. The thing is so certain it need not be said aloud.

## The first oath: by the Day they deny

Ibn Kathir passes over ayah 1 quickly — "Concerning the Day of Judgement, it is well known what it is." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the purpose of an oath is to affirm and emphasise the importance of the subject sworn about; here, that subject is the Resurrection itself.

There is a quiet audacity in this. The rejecters doubt the Day is even possible. Allah swears **by** it — treating it as a fixed, weighty reality already, the way one swears by something no one disputes.

## The second oath: the soul that blames itself

The second thing Allah swears by is far more surprising. *An-nafs al-lawwāmah*.

**The words.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān breaks it open: *nafs* means "soul" or "life"; *lawwāmah* comes from *lawm*, which signifies to reproach or upbraid. So: the self that reproaches itself — the human conscience that scolds a person for the bad he has done.

But the commentary immediately says the scolding does not stop there. This soul "upbraids him not only for doing bad deeds, but also for doing good deeds — *'why did you not do more good, and attain higher stages?'*" In short, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, a perfect believer reproaches himself all the time, whether he has done good or bad. Reproach after sin is quite understandable. Reproach after obedience is the strange part — and it is exactly the point: he should be reaching for higher goals by better deeds, and he upbraids himself for missing out on that score. This interpretation, the commentary says, is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and other leading authorities on tafsir.

**Al-Hasan al-Basri** is the voice the sources return to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that on this same basis he interpreted *nafs lawwāmah* as *nafs mu'minah* — the **believing** soul — and said: "By Allah! A believer at all times upbraids his own self. It is obvious why he should reproach himself when he commits evil. He reproaches himself when he does good deeds as well, because he feels that he has not performed his duties of servitude and Divine worship adequately."

Ibn Kathir preserves another version of al-Hasan's words, through Qurrah bin Khalid, and it is startlingly concrete: "Verily, by Allah, we think that every believer blames himself." Then he shows what that blame sounds like — a man interrogating his own motives: *"What did I intend by my statement? What did I intend by my eating? What did I intend in what I said to myself?"* Then the contrast: **"However, the sinner proceeds ahead and he does not blame himself."**

Hold on to that last line. It is the bridge to ayah 5.

Ibn Kathir gathers three more of the early authorities on the phrase:

- **Saʿīd bin Jubayr** (recorded by Ibn Jarīr): "He criticizes himself in good and bad." Similar is reported from **ʿIkrimah**.
- **Mujāhid** (through Ibn Abī Najīh): "He is sorry for what he missed of good deeds, and he blames himself for it."

**Why swear by such a soul at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers directly: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Hasan al-Basri and others held that Allah swore by the self-reproaching conscience **in order to show honour** for the believing souls who take account of their deeds, who regret and feel sorry for their shortcomings, and who reproach themselves. The oath in ayah 2, the commentary says, lays emphasis on the importance of that conscience and its acceptability in the sight of Allah.

Read the two oaths together and the pairing speaks: the Day on which every deed is finally assessed, and the soul that will not stop assessing its own deeds now.

## Three stages of the self

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to place *lawwāmah* on a map, using terminology it attributes to the noble Sufis, who say that man passes through three stages of human development:

1. **An-nafs al-ammārah** — "the self that tempts (to evil)," as the Qur'an says: *"Surely, man's inner self often incites to evil"* (12:53).
2. **An-nafs al-lawwāmah** — "the self that blames." A person moves from the first stage to this one by performing righteousness and exerting himself in *riyāḍah* (ascetic discipline) and *mujāhadah* (spiritual struggle). This self "is conscious of its own imperfections. It regrets its evils and shortcomings, but it is not completely cut off from the evils."
3. **An-nafs al-muṭma'innah** — "the self at peace." Reached when a person progressively performs righteousness, attains Divine nearness, and applies the sacred laws of the Sharīʿah so rigorously that the Sharīʿah becomes his nature and he develops a natural hatred for anything contrary to it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important point: the interpretation of *lawwāmah* given above **embraces** the *muṭma'innah* as well — the two are titles of a person who fears Allah. The self at peace has not stopped taking itself to account; it has simply made that accounting its nature. So the second stage is not a consolation prize. It is the honour Allah swore by.

## Ayah 3: the objection, quoted back at them

*"Do people think We cannot reassemble their bones?"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this as the disbelievers' oft-repeated objection: once they are dead and reduced to bones and dust, how will they be raised again to life? Ibn Kathir renders the sense of the ayah as: on the Day of Judgement, does he think that We are not able to return his bones and gather them from their various places?

Notice the form of the reply. The Qur'an does not open a philosophical debate. It puts the denial as a **question about the denier** — *does man think…* — turning the spotlight from the doctrine onto the assumption hiding underneath it, and onto the man holding it. And notice what the objection fastens on: bones — which the commentaries describe as decomposed, disintegrated, their particles scattered to different parts of the world.

## Ayah 4: not merely the bones — the fingertips

*"Yes indeed! We are most capable of restoring even their fingertips."*

The answer overturns the denial and then goes further than the objection required.

**Ibn Kathir** paraphrases: does man think We will not gather his bones? Surely We will gather them, and We are quite able to put together his fingertips. "Our power is suitable to gather and recreate them, and if We wished We could surely resurrect him with more than what he originally had. We could make his *banān*, which are the tips of his fingers, all equal in length."

Two shades of meaning sit inside *nusawwiya banānah* in his treatment: to put the fingertips together in perfect order, and — as he spells out — to even them up, making them all equal in length, which goes *beyond* mere restoration. The point is that Allah's power is not straining at the edge of what it can manage. It has room to spare.

**The argument from the first creation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the logic that answers "how?": this has happened once before. Every man who grows and develops in this world has a body composed of particles and elements gathered from different parts of the world. Allah has infinite power; He will gather the disintegrated bones and scattered particles of a man from different parts of the world and give them life again, as He did the first time. To breathe the soul into that structure a second time is no more impossible than it was the first. Why, the commentary asks, should it be surprising? The denier is astonished by a process he is himself the product of.

**Why the fingertips specifically?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons.

*First, because they are among the smallest parts of the body.* If Allah is able to recreate parts that small, with that precision, then recreating the larger limbs — arms, hands, legs, feet — is no difficulty. The argument runs from the delicate to the obvious.

*Second, because the fingertips carry a person's identity.* Allah has characterised every human body with identification marks by which one person is distinctly recognised and distinguished from another. The human face is no more than a few square centimetres, yet no two faces look exactly alike. Human tongues and throats are alike, yet the voices of young and old, of men and women, are easily distinguishable. More amazing still are the fingertips and fingerprints: no two thumbprints or fingerprints are alike, and technical analysis reveals that the patterns of lines are not only on the skin of the thumbs but on the skins of all the fingers — distinguishable and recognisable. Thumbprints have played a decisive role in court decisions and judgments.

The upshot, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: man is amazed at how his bones will be reassembled and given life again, but he should think further than that. He will be raised with the same face, shape and size, and with the same distinctive features — so much so that his fingertips and fingerprints will be reshaped as they were in the first instance of his creation, the same body as in his worldly life without the slightest difference. The commentary closes the passage with the words: *Fa-tabāraka'llāhu aḥsanu'l-khāliqīn* — "Glorious is Allah, the Best of Creators!"

There is something quietly devastating in the choice of *banān*. The thing a person uses to point, to grasp, to press onto a document — the small ridged pattern that has settled cases in court because no other man shares it — is Allah's design and Allah's record. He is not going to lose track of you.

## Ayat 5–6: the argument was never the real reason

*"Still people want to deny what is yet to come, asking mockingly, 'When is this Day of Judgment?'"*

Ayah 5 opens with *bal* — the particle Ibn Kathir's text renders "Nay!" — and it changes everything that came before it. Having answered the objection on its merits, Allah now says: the objection was never where the problem lay.

**What does *li-yafjura amāmah* mean?** The verb *yafjura* is rendered in Ibn Kathir's text as "to break out ahead of himself," and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as wishing "to go on violating Allah's injunctions… ahead of him." In plain English: to break loose from the limits Allah has set and plunge on forward. Ibn Kathir collects the early explanations:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (through Saʿīd): "This means to proceed forward."
- **Mujāhid**: "This means that he wants to proceed ahead following his own whims."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** again (through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah): "This refers to the disbeliever who denies the Day of Reckoning." **Ibn Zayd** said the same.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *amām* as signifying "ahead or future," and reads the ayah this way: the unbeliever, or the unmindful man, does not ponder over the manifestations of Divine Omnipotence — which would lead him to regret his denial in the past and make amends for the future. In fact he wishes to persist in his denial, his polytheism and his sins even in the future.

That is the breaking-loose ayah 5 describes: not one act of rebellion, but a claim staked on the road ahead — *leave my future clear*. He is not weighing the evidence for resurrection; he is protecting a plan. Denial is the tool, not the conclusion.

Now recall al-Hasan al-Basri's line quoted at ayah 2 — the believer stops to interrogate his own intentions, "however, the sinner **proceeds ahead** and he does not blame himself." Ayah 5 shows a man doing exactly that on the scale of a whole life: charging forward, unexamined, with no conscience pulling at his sleeve. Ayah 2's self-reproaching soul and ayah 5's forward-plunging man are the two available ways of facing the future.

**And the question in ayah 6** is not a question. Ibn Kathir is unambiguous: he asks when the Day of Judgement will be, but "his question is only a question of denying its occurrence, and rejecting its existence." A demand for a date, made by someone who has no intention of marking it in his calendar.

Ibn Kathir cites the parallel where Allah answers this same taunt: *"And they say: 'When is this promise, if you are truthful?' Say: 'The appointment to you is for a Day which you cannot put back for an hour, nor put forward'"* (34:29–30). Note what the reply refuses and what it grants. It gives them no date — and it gives them an appointment that cannot be moved by so much as an hour in either direction. The unknown timing is no weakness in the promise; the fixedness of the appointment is the answer.

## Living it

**Build the *lawwāmah*.** Al-Hasan al-Basri's method is available to anyone today, and it is not vague: after speaking, after eating, after your own private thoughts, ask — *what did I intend by that?* Not a general sense of guilt, but a specific question put to a specific act. The sources present this self-questioning as the mark of the believer, and it is what separates him from the man who "proceeds ahead."

**Do not mistake it for despair.** Allah swore by this soul, said Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Hasan al-Basri, to **honour** those who hold themselves to account and feel sorry for their shortcomings. Reproaching yourself even after a good deed — "I could have done more, I could have meant it more" — is not a sickness of the heart. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it as the second stage of a rising path, and one whose meaning carries on into the self at peace.

**Watch the future-tense excuse.** Ayah 5 does not describe a man arguing about theology; it describes a man clearing space in his own life ahead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies the ayah not only to the unbeliever but to "the unmindful man" — so whenever repentance is postponed to a more convenient season, the logic of ayah 5 is operating, quietly, and not only in a denier.

**Let your own hand argue with you.** Every time you press a thumb to unlock a phone, you are using the very evidence ayah 4 chose: a pattern of lines that no other person's finger matches, once already assembled out of particles gathered from across the world — and no more impossible to assemble again than it was the first time.

passages.title: The Day breaks: nowhere to flee but to the Lord
passages.tafsir:
**In brief.** These six ayat are the Qur'an's reply to a question asked in denial. In ayah 6 the man asks, *"When will be this Day of Resurrection?"* — a question, Ibn Kathir says, asked "only… of denying its occurrence, and rejecting its existence." Allah does not answer with a date. He answers with the scene itself: the sight fails, the moon loses its light, the sun and moon are joined together — and the man who asked the question is suddenly looking for somewhere to run.

What holds the passage together is a single movement, from the sky to the self. Ayat 7–9 describe what happens to the universe; ayat 10–12 describe what happens to a human being standing inside it. The cosmos goes dark, the human being wants to flee, and the passage lands on one word of destination: **ilā rabbika** — *unto your Lord.*

## The question these ayat are answering

To feel the force of ayah 7 you have to hear what came just before it. Ibn Kathir explains that the surah opens with an oath — *"Nay! I swear by the Day of Resurrection"* — and notes a point of Arabic usage he has covered elsewhere: when the thing sworn about is something being **denied**, it is permissible to place *lā* ("Nay") before the oath to emphasise the negation. Qatadah said the sense is simply, "I swear by both of these things," and the same has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid bin Jubayr. What is being sworn about, Ibn Kathir says, is "the affirmation of the final abode and the refutation against the claim of the ignorant that the resurrection of bodies will not occur."

Then comes the portrait of the man in ayah 5. On *"Man desires to break out ahead of himself,"* Ibn ʿAbbas said it means "to proceed forward"; Mujahid said, "he wants to proceed ahead following his own whims." In another report, ʿAli bin Abi Talhah relates from Ibn ʿAbbas that this refers to "the disbeliever who denies the Day of Reckoning" — and Ibn Zayd said the same. Ibn Kathir then joins ayah 6 directly to that portrait: "Thus, Allah says after this, *He asks: 'When will be this Day of Resurrection?'*" So the questioner is that man, and Ibn Kathir is blunt about what kind of question he is asking: "His question is only a question of denying its occurrence, and rejecting its existence." He compares it to Allah's words elsewhere: *"And they say: 'When is this promise if you are truthful?' Say: 'The appointment to you is for a Day, which you cannot put back for an hour nor put forward'"* (34:29–30).

Immediately after quoting that, Ibn Kathir writes, "Here Allah says: *fa-idhā bariqa al-baṣar*." Ayah 7 opens with *fa-idhā* — "So, when…" You asked *when*? Here is when. Not a calendar; a collapse.

## Ayah 7 — the sight that cannot hold still

*Fa-idhā bariqa al-baṣar* — "But when the sight is stunned."

Ibn Kathir preserves two ways this verb was recited.

**The first: *bariqa*, with a kasrah** — the short vowel *i*, marked under the letter *rā'*. This is how Abu ʿAmr bin al-ʿAlā' recited it, and Ibn Kathir says it carries the sense of the sight being *diminished*. To illustrate it he reaches for another ayah: *"Their gaze returning not towards them"* (14:43) — and glosses it vividly: "they will be looking this way and that way in horror. Their gaze will not be able to rest upon anything due to the severity of the terror on that Day."

Picture it exactly as described. The eye is open and moving, darting from one thing to the next, and it cannot land. There is no object in that landscape safe enough to settle on. The horror is not that the eye is closed; it is that it will not stop.

**The second: *baraqa*, with a fatḥah** — the short vowel *a*, marked over the same letter. Ibn Kathir says its meaning "is close to the first recitation," and then gives the intent of the ayah: "the eyes will be dazzled, humbled, diminished, and humiliated on the Day of Judgement due to the severity of the horrors and the greatness of the matters that they will witness on that Day." Notice how much is in that list. These are not merely frightened eyes; they are eyes brought low.

Maarif ul Quran takes the verb the same way: *bariqa* means, of the eyes, "to be dazzled and unable to see." And it makes the scope universal — "On the Day of Resurrection, the eyes of all will be dazzled and will not be able to see consistently." Not the eyes of the wicked only. Every eye.

And there is a quiet justice in it. The man of ayah 6 wanted the Day produced for his inspection. When it arrives, the first thing the passage takes from him is his sight.

## Ayat 8–9 — the lights go out

*Wa khasafa al-qamar* — "and the moon is dimmed." Ibn Kathir's gloss is five words: "its light will go away." Maarif ul Quran traces the verb: *khasafa* comes from *khusūf*, which means "to lose light and become dark" — the moon will lose its light, or be eclipsed.

*Wa jumiʿa al-shamsu wa al-qamar* — "and the sun and the moon are brought together." Mujahid said of this, "They will be rolled up." Explaining the ayah, Ibn Zayd recited a passage from another surah: *"When the sun is wound round and its light is lost and is overthrown, and when the stars fall"* (81:1–2). And it has been reported from Ibn Masʿud that he recited the ayah with a slight variation — *wa jumiʿa bayna al-shamsi wa al-qamar*, "and the sun and the moon will be joined **between** each other."

Maarif ul Quran draws out why ayah 9 matters after ayah 8. The moon losing its light is one thing; the *joining*, it says, "signifies that not only the moon will lose its light, but also the sun will be eclipsed." It adds an observation from natural science: astronomers have discovered that the sun has the original light, while the light of the moon is borrowed from the sun. So on that Day, it explains, the two will be fused together and **both** will lose their lights. Follow that logic and you see what is being described. Not a shadow crossing a borrowed light while the source keeps burning — the source itself goes out.

Maarif ul Quran then reports a second interpretation with proper caution: "Some scholars interpret this statement to mean that on that Day the sun and the moon will rise from the same point, as some narratives report. And Allah know best!" That closing phrase is the model to follow — where the scholars differed on how the joining will occur, the source holds both readings and hands the certainty back to Allah.

Take the three ayat together and see what has been dismantled. Sight, moonlight, sunlight — every means by which a human being orients himself in the world. Before a single word of judgement is spoken, the lights are simply switched off.

## Ayah 10 — the question changes from "when" to "where"

*"On that Day one will cry, 'Where is the escape?'"*

Ibn Kathir's explanation is almost cinematic: "the human will see these horrors on the Day of Judgement and he will want to flee. He will say, 'Where is the place to flee to?' This means, where is the escape or refuge?"

Watch the word the Qur'an uses for the one speaking here: *al-insān* — "man," the human being. It is the same word that stood over ayah 3, *"Does man think that We shall not assemble his bones?"*, and over ayah 5, *"Nay! Man desires to break out ahead of himself"* — the man Ibn ʿAbbas identified as "the disbeliever who denies the Day of Reckoning," and the man Ibn Kathir says goes on to ask the question of ayah 6.

So the question has changed shape. In ayah 6 it was *ayyāna* — *when?* — asked, Ibn Kathir says, to deny that the Day would come at all. In ayah 10 it is *ayna* — *where?* — and now it is not a debating point. It is what a man says when he wants to run. He has stopped arguing about whether the Day exists and started looking for the exits.

## Ayah 11 — *kallā*, there is no refuge

*Kallā lā wazar* — "But no! There will be no refuge." Ibn Kathir renders *kallā* simply: "No!" The plea of ayah 10 is refused as soon as it is voiced.

On *lā wazar*, Ibn Kathir reports something striking: Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid bin Jubayr "and several others of the Salaf" — the earliest generations of Muslims — all said, "There will be no salvation." He compares it with Allah's words, *"You will have no refuge on that Day nor there will be for you any denying"* (42:47), which he explains as "there will be no place for you to hide," and he glosses *lā wazar* here as "there will be no place for you to seek shelter."

Sit with how total that is. Every refuge a person has ever used — distance, wealth, status, a crowd to hide in, an argument to hide behind, even the simple animal option of running — is gone in three words of Arabic. Not because flight is difficult, but because, as Ibn Kathir puts it, there is no place left to hide and no shelter left to reach.

## Ayah 12 — the one place left

*Ilā rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr* — "On that Day all will end up before your Lord." Ibn Kathir: "meaning, the place of return and the final destination."

Here the passage turns on a beautiful piece of construction — and you can see it in Ibn Kathir's own two glosses. Ayah 10 asks for *al-mafarr*, which he explains as "the place to flee to." Ayah 12 answers with *al-mustaqarr*, which he explains as "the place of return and the final destination." Both are a *place*; and the second cancels the first by giving what the first was really after. He wanted somewhere to end up. He gets somewhere to end up. It is simply not the somewhere he had in mind.

Notice too the word the ayah chooses for Allah: *rabbika*, **your Lord** — and notice that it is in the second person. The verse does not say "unto Him" or "unto their Lord." It turns and addresses the reader, so that whoever is reciting is placed in the scene alongside the man being described.

On what "unto your Lord" means, we say what Ibn Kathir said and no more: it is the place of return and the final destination. Allah is affirmed as He described Himself, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying His words of their meaning.

The very next ayah, which falls just outside this passage, completes the thought: on that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind — Ibn Kathir says he will be told of "all of his deeds, the old of them and the recent of them, the first of them and the last of them, the small of them and the large of them."

## Living it

Read these six ayat slowly and you notice they take away, one by one, every place a person hides. The eye that could always find something to rest on will not rest. The lights in the sky go out. The instinct to run finds no direction worth running in. And what is left is not a void but a destination — *ilā rabbika*, the place of return.

That is why the passage is not asking us to fear an unmapped terror. It is telling us where we are already going, and letting us decide how we would like to arrive.

The surah itself, a few ayat earlier, has already named the habit that prepares a person for that arrival. Allah swears by *al-nafs al-lawwāmah*, the self-reproaching soul, and Ibn Kathir records al-Hasan al-Basri's description of it: "Verily, by Allah, we think that every believer blames himself. He says, questioning himself, 'What did I intend by my statement? What did I intend by my eating? What did I intend in what I said to myself?' However, the sinner proceeds ahead and he does not blame himself." Mujahid described the same soul as one who "is sorry for what he missed of good deeds and he blames himself for it," and Saʿid bin Jubayr said, "He criticizes himself in good and bad."

Set that beside ayat 10–12 and the lesson is exact. There are two ways to face your Lord: to examine yourself now, while the examination is still voluntary — or to reach the *mustaqarr* having never once asked yourself what you intended. Al-Hasan's small, honest question at the end of a day — *what did I actually intend by that?* — is the whole practice. And the reason to take it up is in ayah 12 itself: the return is to your Lord either way. The only thing still in your hands is whether you walk toward that destination now, or are brought to it then with your eyes darting and nowhere to hide.

passages.title: The record disclosed and the self that testifies
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat come immediately after the announcement that on the Day of Resurrection there is nowhere left to run: "No! There is no refuge! Unto your Lord will be the place of rest that Day" (ayat 11–12) — which Ibn Kathir explains as "the place of return and the final destination." Flight is over; what follows is the account. A person is handed the full record of his life (ayah 13); then, before he can plead ignorance, the Qur'an cuts in: he was never in the dark about himself (ayah 14), whatever excuses he offers (ayah 15). The thread holding them together is a single idea: **on that Day, knowledge of your life is not something withheld from you and then revealed — it is something you already carry, now made public.**

## Ayah 13: "what he sent forward, and what he left behind"

يُنَبَّؤُاْ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنُ يَوۡمَئِذِۭ بِمَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ

*"On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind."*

Ibn Kathir glosses this broadly: "he will be informed of all of his deeds, the old of them and the recent of them, the first of them and the last of them, the small of them and the large of them." Nothing is filtered out for being ancient, and nothing is dropped for being trivial. He supports this with Allah's words about the record: "And they will find all that they did, placed before them, and your Lord treats no one with injustice" (18:49).

Then come the two words the ayah turns on: **مَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ** — what he sent forward and what he left behind. The commentators read this pair in more than one way, and each reading opens a different window.

**1. Deeds done, and the legacy that outlives you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās that "what he sent ahead" refers to the good deeds a person dispatched before his death, while "what he left behind" refers to "the good or bad, useful or harmful custom he invented and left behind which people follow. He will continue to receive its reward or punishment."

Sit with that. Your ledger does not close when you are buried. A practice you started — a way of doing things you made normal for your family, your friends, your workplace, whoever imitated you — keeps running after you, and it keeps writing into your account in both directions. The good habit you planted in a child, and equally the shortcut or the cruelty you made look acceptable to somebody watching.

**2. What you did, and what you failed to do.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also gives Qatādah's reading: "what he sent ahead" is a good deed a person did in his lifetime, and "what he left behind" is "a good deed he could have done but did not do and wasted his time or opportunity."

On this reading the ayah reckons not only with wrong committed but with good *delayed* — the charity postponed, the reconciliation never attempted, the years spent on nothing. Both readings are transmitted from the early authorities; neither cancels the other, and together they widen the ayah rather than narrowing it.

Set alongside Ibn Kathir's "the first of them and the last of them, the small of them and the large of them," the picture is of an account that reaches backwards into forgotten years and forwards past the grave.

## Ayah 14: "Rather — man is a witness against himself"

بَلِ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنُ عَلَىٰ نَفۡسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٞ

Ibn Kathir renders it "Nay! Man will be well informed about himself"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "Rather, man will be a witness against himself." Either way the ayah opens with a turn — *this informing is not because he needs to be told.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes exactly that point. Being shown the record, it says, is "for purposes of following the procedures of fairness and justice" — man will be shown each of his deeds on the Plain of Reckoning — "although in fact this will not be necessary for him, because every man knows what he does in this world, and he will recall his deeds in the Hereafter, even though he will make excuses." It adds that he will see all his good and bad actions there, quoting again: "And they will find what they did all there" (18:49). The record is published so that justice is *seen* to be done. The knowledge itself was already his.

### The word *baṣīrah*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key term. One meaning of *baṣīrah* is simply **"to see."** Another meaning is **"evidence"** — as in Allah's words, *"There have come to you evidences from your Lord"* (6:104), where the word rendered "evidences," *baṣāʾir*, is the plural of *baṣīrah* and means "evidence, proof, argument or insight." (A note there records that "insights" is the sense on which Muhammad Taqi Usmani renders 6:104.)

Both senses land on the same devastating point, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws them out in turn:

- Take *baṣīrah* as **seeing**, and the ayah says: a person is clear-eyed about himself. He sees what he has been.
- Take *baṣīrah* as **evidence**, and the ayah says: "man will be a clear proof against himself, in spite of any excuses he might offer." He is not merely the defendant. He is the exhibit.

Ibn Kathir arrives at the same place: "he will be a witness against himself, knowing full well what he did, even though he will try to make excuses and deny it." He cites Allah's words to the one handed his book: **"Read your book. You are sufficient as a reckoner against yourself this Day"** (17:14). Qatādah's comment on our ayah is a single line — "This means he is a witness against himself."

### The limbs as evidence

ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained *"Nay! Man will be well informed about himself"* by listing: **"His hearing, his sight, his two hands, his two legs and his limbs."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion — a man "fails to realize that in this situation, the limbs of his own body — his hearing, his sight, his two hands and his two legs — will testify against him."

This is worth pausing over. The evidence against a person is not an external file assembled by strangers. It is his own body — the ears that chose what to listen to, the eyes that chose what to look at, the hands and feet that carried him where he went. The instruments of the deed become the testimony to it.

### A warning aimed at us, not at "them"

Ibn Kathir preserves a second narration from Qatādah on this ayah that turns the blade inward: **"By Allah! If you wish to see him, you would see him as someone who sees the shortcomings of the people and their sins, yet he is heedless of his own sins."**

Ibn Kathir follows it with a saying that circulated among the early Muslims — "It used to be said, 'Verily, it is written in the Injīl: O Son of Adam, do you see the small splinters in the eye of your brother and disregard the tree stump that is in your eye, so you do not see it?'"

The irony is sharp: ayah 14 says a person has *baṣīrah* — sight, insight — regarding himself, and Qatādah observes that in this life we aim that sight everywhere except at ourselves. The faculty exists. We simply point it outward. On that Day it will finally be turned where it belonged.

## Ayah 15: "though he may put forth his excuses"

وَلَوۡ أَلۡقَىٰ مَعَاذِيرَهُۥ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies **مَعَاذِير** (*maʿādhīr*) as the plural of *miʿdhār*, meaning "excuse," and renders the phrase "even though he may offer his excuses"; Ibn Kathir has "though he may put forth his excuses." The "even though" is the hinge: the testimony of ayah 14 stands **regardless**.

The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir read the phrase in complementary ways:

- **Mujāhid:** "even though he argues in defense of it, he is a witness against it." The excuses do not touch the fact of his own testimony.
- **Qatādah:** "Even though he will try to make false excuses on that Day, they will not be accepted from him."
- **As-Suddī:** "This means his argument."
- **Al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās:** "This is apologizing" — and Ibn ʿAbbās then asks, "Haven't you heard that Allah said, *'The Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers'* (40:52)?" In the same statement he goes on to recite *"And they will offer submission to Allah on that Day"* (16:87), *"Then they will (falsely) submit: 'We used not to do any evil'"* (16:28), and *"By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah"* (6:23).

Ibn Kathir himself sets alongside As-Suddī's comment the Qur'an's own record of what these excuses sound like:

- **"There will then be no Fitnah for them but to say: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah'"** (6:23) — sworn under oath, on the Day when the truth is plain.
- **"On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all together; then they will swear to Him as they swear to you (O Muslims). And they think that they have something. Verily, they are liars!"** (58:18) — the habit of lying persists into the Hereafter itself.

Read together, ayat 14 and 15 form one sentence with a hinge: *he is his own evidence — and no amount of talking changes that.* On Mujāhid's reading the excuse-making does not even work as a strategy that fails at the last moment; a man argues in his own defence and remains, in the same breath, a witness against himself.

## Living it

**Audit the two columns now.** Ayah 13 names *what you sent forward* and *what you left behind*. On the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, ask what practices you are leaving running behind you — what people copy from you, for which reward or punishment keeps arriving. On Qatādah's reading, ask what good you keep postponing. Both are being recorded today.

**Nothing is too small or too old to appear.** Ibn Kathir's "the small of them and the large of them, the first of them and the last of them" cuts both ways — it should unsettle us about forgotten wrongs and encourage us about forgotten kindnesses. And with it stands the promise of 18:49 that Ibn Kathir cites: *"your Lord treats no one with injustice."*

**Turn the sight inward before it is turned for you.** Qatādah's warning about the man alert to everyone's faults but his own, and the saying about the splinter and the tree stump, are the practical heart of this passage. The *baṣīrah* — the seeing, the clear evidence — is already yours; the only question is whether you use it on yourself now, voluntarily, or meet it on the Day when your own hearing, sight, hands and legs speak.

**Drop the excuses early.** If, as Mujāhid says, a defence offered there does not stop a person from being a witness against himself, and if, as Qatādah says, false excuses will not be accepted, then honest admission in this life is the only argument worth preparing. Excuses are the one thing this passage guarantees will be useless.

passages.title: Do not rush the tongue with revelation
passages.tafsir:
In the middle of a sūrah about the Resurrection, Allah turns aside from the terrors of that Day to speak privately to His Messenger ﷺ about something else entirely: how to receive revelation. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, up to this point the sūrah had been describing the conditions and horrors of the Day of Resurrection; these next four ayat are a special guidance for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to follow at the time of revelation.

What holds them together is a single exchange of responsibility. Ayah 16 tells the Prophet ﷺ what to stop doing. Ayat 17–19 tell him what Allah will do instead. Twice the passage says *inna ʿalaynā* — "it is upon Us" — once in ayah 17 and once in ayah 19, with the instruction of ayah 18 held between them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up what Allah has taken upon Himself: collecting it in his heart, making him recite it, and conveying it to the people. And it sums up the message to him in a sentence: do not worry about all this; it is Our concern.

## The moment behind the words

Ibn Kathir opens his comment with one sentence that unlocks the whole passage: this is Allah teaching His Messenger ﷺ how to receive the revelation from the angel.

Picture what was actually happening. Jibrīl would descend with a portion of the Qur'an and begin reciting. The Prophet ﷺ, Ibn Kathir says, was rushing in his attempts to grasp the revelation, reciting it along with the angel while the angel was still reciting it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the two fears driving that urgency. First, that there might be some discrepancy between his listening and his reciting it back. Second, that he might forget some portion of it, or that some word might escape his memory. So when Jibrīl recited a verse, he would exert himself in repeating the words immediately upon hearing them — and in this manner, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the strain would be multiplied.

Notice what this tells us about the Prophet ﷺ. This was not carelessness; it was the opposite. It was the anxiety of a man entrusted with the speech of his Lord who could not bear the thought of losing one word of it. Allah's correction here is a correction of method, not of sincerity — and the reassurance that follows is offered to a heart that was straining out of love for what it carried.

**A gesture preserved in the chain of narration.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to struggle very hard to grasp the revelation and used to move his lips rapidly with the recitation. Then something remarkable happens inside the narration itself. The narrator, Saʿīd, reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said to him: *I will move my lips like the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to move his lips* — and demonstrated. Then the subnarrator reports that Saʿīd said to him: *I will move my lips like I saw Ibn ʿAbbās moving his lips* — and demonstrated in turn. A physical movement, not only a wording, was handed on from one narrator to the next, so that we could see the moment rather than only read about it. Ibn Kathir notes that this has also been recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Then the ayat came down. And the change in the Prophet's ﷺ conduct was immediate. Al-Bukhari's wording, as Ibn Kathir cites it, says: whenever Jibrīl would come to him he would be silent, and when Jibrīl had left he would recite it just as Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, had promised him.

Silence during, recitation after. That is the whole method, and it worked because Allah had promised it would.

## "It is upon Us" — what Allah takes upon Himself

The passage turns on a single phrase, repeated. Our translation of ayah 17 renders it "It is certainly upon Us"; ayah 19, "Then it is surely upon Us." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "It is surely undertaken by Us." Ibn Kathir's rendering is "It is for Us." Either way, the Prophet ﷺ is being told that the task has been transferred. Strain is unnecessary because the outcome no longer rests on his effort.

**Ayah 16 — *lā tuḥarrik bihi lisānak*.** "Do not move your tongue with it." Notice that the "it" is a bare pronoun — the Qur'an is not named in the ayah at all. Ibn Kathir supplies the referent: it means with the Qur'an.

*Li-taʿjala bihi* — "so as to hasten with it," or in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering, "so as you receive it in hurry." What the ayah forbids is tied to the haste behind the movement. Ibn Kathir places alongside it a parallel instruction from elsewhere in the Qur'an: "And be not in haste with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say: 'My Lord! Increase me in knowledge'" (20:114). That pairing is instructive. The alternative to grabbing is not passivity — it is a prayer for more knowledge. Stop snatching; start asking.

**Ayah 17 — *jamʿahu wa qurʼānah*.** Ibn Kathir explains "It is for Us to collect it" as meaning: in your chest. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same undertaking as storing it in your heart. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration quoted above, glosses it the same way — He will collect it in his chest to recite it. The memorising is Allah's work, not the Prophet's ﷺ.

Then *qurʼānah* — "and that it be recited." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the key linguistic point plainly: **the word *qurʼān* here means "recitation."** So what Allah undertakes in ayah 17 is not only to store it, but, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that you recite it — and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrasing, to let it be recited by him after the revelation is completed.

**Ayah 18 — *fa-idhā qaraʼnāhu fattabiʿ qurʼānah*.** "So when We have recited it, follow its recitation." Ibn Kathir glosses "when We have recited it to you" as: when the angel has recited it to you from Allah.

And what does "follow" mean? Both sources agree, and it is not what one might first assume. It does not mean *recite along with him*. Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as: listen to it and pay attention. Ibn Kathir: listen to it, then recite it as he taught you to recite it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that by the general consensus of the scholars the phrase means: when Jibrīl recites, be silent and listen to it — following, in its rendering, by concentration of the heart. The command to *follow* is, in the first instance, a command to receive. Reproduction comes afterwards: as Ibn ʿAbbās's narration continues, when Jibrīl would leave, he would recite it as Jibrīl had taught him to recite it.

**Ayah 19 — *thumma inna ʿalaynā bayānah*.** "Then it is surely upon Us to make it clear." The *thumma* ("then") marks a further stage: Ibn Kathir explains that this comes after memorising it and reciting it — that Allah will explain it to him, clarify it, and inspire him with its meaning according to what Allah intended and legislated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it just as strongly: it is Allah's concern to explain the true message of the verses; the meaning of every single word of the Qur'an will be made plain to the Prophet ﷺ, and he need not be concerned about it.

## Three stages, and why the order matters

Ibn Kathir draws the passage into a clean sequence. The first phase was gathering it in his chest. The second phase was recitation. The third phase was its explanation and the clarification of its meaning.

Sound, then speech, then sense. Allah does not ask His Messenger ﷺ to secure the words *and* work out the meaning in the same anxious instant. He separates the tasks and takes them on Himself. What the Prophet ﷺ contributes at the moment of revelation is attentive silence.

And notice how precisely Ibn Kathir words the third stage: Allah would inspire him with its meaning *according to what We intended and legislated*. The understanding of the Book was not left to the Prophet ﷺ to construct on his own; it was itself given, and given in conformity with what Allah meant by it.

## Why these four ayat sit inside a sūrah about the Resurrection

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question a careful reader will already be asking: what is the contextual relationship between these four ayat and the rest of the sūrah, in the middle of which they are set? Its answer is one of the most beautiful things in the commentary on this passage.

Look at what came immediately before. The sūrah had been arguing that every man will be resurrected in the same state, the same shape and size in which he was created the first time — his fingertips reconstructed with the same precision as the first time, his fingerprints redesigned with the same patterns of lines on their skin as before, without a hair's breadth of difference. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is possible only because Allah is Omniscient: His knowledge is infinite and all-encompassing, and His preserving capacity is incomparable, unparalleled and unique.

And it is on the basis of those attributes, it continues, that these four ayat were revealed to console and comfort the Prophet ﷺ. The argument runs: *You can forget, and it is possible that you could make a mistake in transmission. But Allah is beyond these things.* The same knowledge that can restore the pattern of lines on a fingertip can hold the words of a sūrah intact in a human heart.

So the passage is not a digression at all. It is the sūrah's own teaching about Allah, turned around and applied as a personal mercy to the man carrying its message. And once the point is made, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the sūrah reverts to its basic theme of Resurrection and resumes describing the conditions of the Hereafter.

## A ruling scholars drew from ayah 18

Because ayah 18 establishes that "following" a recitation means falling silent and listening, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects it to the position of the one praying behind an imam.

The principle of congregational prayer, it explains, is that the *muqtadī* — the one who follows the imam — follows him: when he bows, they bow; when he prostrates, they prostrate. But recitation, the commentary argues, is the one place where following takes the opposite form. In line with this principle, it notes, a hadith in Sahih Muslim adds: "When he [the imam] recites, be silent and listen."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents this as the argument of Imam Abu Hanifah and some other imams in holding that those praying behind an imam should not recite. It is careful to name whose argument it is rather than to present it as everyone's, and it closes the discussion with "And Allah knows best" — the customary acknowledgement that this is a matter of scholarly reasoning. What the passage itself establishes is the underlying principle: attentive silence is a genuine form of following.

## Living it

**Receive before you reproduce.** The Prophet's ﷺ instinct — to reach for the words as they arrived, out of fear of losing them — is a deeply human instinct, and Allah redirected it. The exertion multiplied the strain rather than securing the outcome. When you sit with the Qur'an, the first act is to listen to it and pay attention, exactly as Ibn ʿAbbās glossed ayah 18. The retaining follows.

**Memorisation and understanding are gifts, not achievements.** Ayah 17 assigns the collecting of the Qur'an in the chest to Allah, and ayah 19 assigns its explanation to Allah. A student of the Qur'an works hard, but knows Who is actually doing the work. And Ibn Kathir's cross-reference gives the student his own supplication: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge" (20:114).

**Trust the guarantee.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary of these four ayat is the sentence to carry away: Allah has taken upon Himself the responsibility of storing the words of the Qur'an in the Prophet's ﷺ heart and of explaining its message to him. Do not worry about all this — it is Our concern. And in Al-Bukhari's wording, when Jibrīl had left, he would recite it just as Allah had promised him. The Book you hold is the keeping of that promise.

passages.title: The fleeting world and the faces that will gaze at their Lord
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** After four ayat spoken to the Prophet ﷺ about how the Qur'an would be gathered in his chest and made clear to him, the sūrah turns back to its main business: the Day of Resurrection. Ayat 20–21 name the reason people push that Day away — not an argument, but an appetite. Ayat 22–25 then show where that appetite ends: two sets of faces on the Day itself, one radiant and looking toward its Lord, one gloomy and certain of what is about to land on it. Love of the fleeting now, neglect of the lasting then — and the two faces those two loves produce.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to raise a question about arrangement: what is the contextual relationship between those four ayat (16–19) and the rest of a sūrah about the Resurrection? Its answer makes ayah 20 land properly.

Before those four ayat, while describing the Resurrection, it had been made plain that Allah's knowledge is infinite — so much so that every man will be raised in the same state, the same shape and size in which he was created the first time, his fingertips reconstructed with the same precision and his fingerprints redesigned with the same patterns of lines as before, without a hair's breadth of difference. That is possible, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, only because Allah is Omniscient, His knowledge all-encompassing, and His preserving capacity incomparable and unique.

It was on the basis of those very attributes that the four ayat came to console the Prophet ﷺ. He is told: you can forget, and it is possible that you could make a mistake in transmission — but Allah is beyond these things. Allah has taken upon Himself the responsibility of storing the words of the Qur'an in your heart and of explaining the message to you. Do not worry about it; it is His concern. The same knowledge that will reassemble a man's fingerprints will keep the Qur'an intact in the Prophet's ﷺ chest.

Then, with that settled, the sūrah reverts to its basic theme and resumes its description of the conditions and horrors of the Hereafter. **Ayah 20 is that resumption**, and it opens by turning to face the deniers directly.

## "But no!" — the real reason for denial (20–21)

The ayah opens with **كَلَّا (kallā)**, rendered here "But no!", followed by **بَلْ (bal)**, "In fact" — Ibn Kathir's text reads "But no! Rather you love the present life of this world." First a denial; then what is put in its place. And what is put in its place is startling: not a proof, but a diagnosis of the heart.

Ibn Kathir states it plainly. The only thing that has caused them to reject the Day of Judgement, and to oppose the true revelation and the Mighty Qur'an that Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ, is that **their only concern is the present worldly life**. They are preoccupied, and distracted from the Hereafter.

Read that again, because it reframes the whole argument of the sūrah. What came before was evidence — the reconstruction of a man in the same shape and size, down to the lines on his fingertips. Yet when Allah names the cause of rejection, He does not say "you have not understood," or "you have weighed the evidence badly." He says **you love**. The obstacle Ibn Kathir identifies is not a failure of information but a preoccupation — an attention already spent elsewhere.

**The two verbs are worth feeling.** In ayah 20 the object of love is **الْعَاجِلَة (al-ʿājilah)** — rendered here "this fleeting world," and by Ibn Kathir "the present life of this world." Then ayah 21: **وَتَذَرُونَ الْآخِرَة**, "and you neglect the Hereafter" — you leave it, you let it lie. Notice the asymmetry: the Hereafter is not attacked, argued with, or disproved. It is simply left while attention goes elsewhere. Ibn Kathir's two words for it are *preoccupied* and *distracted*, and neither of those is a decision anyone announces.

Notice too that the address is **"you"** — plural, direct, in your face, where the four ayat just before it had been addressed to the Prophet ﷺ alone. This is not a report about some distant nation. It is a question put to whoever is reciting: where does your love actually go, and what have you quietly left unattended?

## The Day, told through faces

From ayah 22 the sūrah stops describing the Day and starts describing *people* on it — and it does so entirely through faces. Ibn Kathir shows this is a recurring Qur'anic method by lining up the parallels: "On the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black" (3:106); "Some faces that Day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing at the good news. And other faces, that Day will be dust-stained; darkness will cover them, such will be the disbelieving, wicked" (80:38–42); and the pairing in Sūrah al-Ghāshiyah between faces "humiliated, labouring, weary" who enter the hot blazing Fire (88:2–4) and faces "joyful, happy with their endeavour, in a lofty Paradise" (88:8–10).

The face is where the inner state becomes public. On that Day, what a person loved will no longer be a private matter; it will be legible on him.

## Faces radiant — and what they are looking at (22–23)

**نَاضِرَة (nāḍirah).** Ibn Kathir traces it to the word **naḍārah**, which he glosses as splendid, radiant, glowing, delighted with goodness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the word as "fresh" — many faces that day will be happy, fresh and radiant. Freshness and delight together; Ibn Kathir's phrase "delighted with goodness" catches both halves at once.

And the sūrah does not leave the radiance unexplained. It puts the cause in the very next ayah.

**إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ — "looking at their Lord."** Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it is the heart of this passage: *they will see Him with their very eyes.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees — "looking towards their Lord" means "gazing at their Lord," and this proves that the inmates of Paradise will see Allah in the Hereafter with physical eyes.

## The vision of Allah: what the Sunnah says

Ibn Kathir does not leave this as a claim; he gathers the evidence, and it is worth walking through, because he considers the matter closed: the believers seeing Allah in the abode of the Hereafter has been confirmed in the authentic hadiths from numerous routes of transmission with the scholars of hadith, and it is not possible to deny this or refuse it.

- **Al-Bukhari records in his Sahih** the words of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Verily, you all will see your Lord with your own eyes."*
- **The hadiths of Abu Saʿīd and Abu Hurayrah, both recorded in the Two Sahihs**: some people said, "O Messenger of Allah! Will we see our Lord on the Day of Judgement?" The Prophet ﷺ said, *"Are you harmed by seeing the sun and the moon when there are no clouds beneath them?"* They replied, "No." The Prophet ﷺ then said, *"Then you will surely see your Lord like that."*
- **From Jābir, in the Two Sahihs**: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at the moon on a night when it was full, and said, *"Verily, you will see your Lord just as you see this moon! So if you are able to avoid missing a prayer before the rising of the sun (Fajr prayer) or before its setting (ʿAsr prayer), then do so."*
- **From Suhayb — among the hadiths which Muslim was alone in recording**: when the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah will say, "Do you want Me to give you anything extra?" They will say, "Haven't You whitened our faces? Haven't You entered us into Paradise and saved us from the Fire?" Then He will remove the veil — *and they will not be given anything more beloved to them than looking at their Lord.* That is the **Ziyādah**, the "extra." The Prophet ﷺ then recited: "For those who have done good is the best and extra (Ziyādah)" (10:26).
- **From Jābir — also among the hadiths which Muslim was alone in recording**: *"Verily, Allah will appear before the believers while He is laughing."*

That last narration, and the comparison to the sun and the moon before it, raise the obvious question of *how* such a sight can be. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes that question up directly, and we come to it below.

One thing is worth pausing over in the Suhayb narration, because the narration itself makes the point: the people of Paradise, offered more, answer by listing what they have already been given — whitened faces, entry into Paradise, rescue from the Fire. And Allah still has something further to give. When it comes, it is nothing they had thought to name, and nothing more beloved to them than it: looking at their Lord.

**Where and how often.** Ibn Kathir notes that this will take place on the open plains of the Resurrection place, adding that some of these hadiths mention the believers looking at their Lord on the open plains, and some mention that this will occur in the Gardens of Paradise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī, adds that the inmates of Paradise will occupy different positions, and consequently some will see Allah on a weekly basis, on Fridays; others will see Him daily, morning and evening; and yet others will see Him all the time, under all conditions. Different positions in Paradise, on that report, mean different measures of this.

**Where the scholars stood.** Ibn Kathir writes that this is something the Companions, the Successors and the Salaf of this nation have agreed upon, and that it is agreed upon between the Imams of Islam and the guides of all mankind. He adds that were it not for fear of taking up a lot of space, he would present all of these hadiths with their routes of transmission and wordings from those that are in the Sahih collections, the collections of good narrations, the Musnad collections and the Sunan collections — and he notes that he has mentioned this in separate places in his Tafsir.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the scholars of Ahlus-Sunnah — those following the classic way of interpreting the religion — are unanimous on this issue, and names the dissent: **the Muʿtazilites and the Khārijites deny the possibility of seeing Allah, even in Paradise.** Their reasoning, it says, is philosophical scepticism: they say there are certain conditions of distance that must be met between the one who sees with his physical eyes and the object that is seen, and that these conditions cannot be met between the Creator and the created. The Ahlus-Sunnah respond that in the Hereafter the vision of Allah will be **beyond the need of these conditions**: He will be seen, unlike any material being, beyond space, direction, shape or form.

That reply is the balance the Salaf held, and it is worth stating in both directions. We **affirm** what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ affirmed — real sight, with the eyes, as Ibn Kathir says with their very eyes and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says with physical eyes — and we do not empty it out into a metaphor for knowledge or expectation. And we equally refuse to picture it or to ask *how*, because the One seen is beyond space, direction, shape and form, and is not like anything in the creation. Affirmation without likeness; acceptance without interrogation.

## Faces gloomy — and the dread that is not a guess (24–25)

Then the other half of humanity, and the sūrah's mood drops in a single word.

**بَاسِرَة (bāsirah).** Ibn Kathir heads this section "Blackening of the Faces of the Disobedient People on the Day of Judgement," and says plainly: these are the faces of the sinners. **Qatādah** glossed *bāsirah* as "gloomy." **As-Suddī** said their colour will change. Whatever brightness a face had drains out of it.

**تَظُنُّ (taẓunnu).** The renderings give it as "thinking" and "anticipating" — words that in English leave room for guesswork. Ibn Kathir closes that room in three words: **"meaning, they will be certain."** This is not anxious speculation. It is knowledge that has arrived too late to be any use.

Certain of what? **فَاقِرَة (fāqirah)**, rendered here "something devastating," and in Ibn Kathir's text "some calamity." The early authorities he cites each reach for a different edge of it: **Mujāhid** said "a disaster"; **Qatādah** said "an evil"; **As-Suddī** said they will be certain that they are going to be destroyed; **Ibn Zayd** said they will think that they are going to enter into the Hellfire.

And notice the timing of the ruin: it is *about to* fall on them. Ayah 25 does not describe the punishment; it describes the moment of knowing it is coming. The dread arrives before the Fire does. Set the two halves side by side and the symmetry is in the faces: on one side, radiance and a Lord already being looked at; on the other, gloom and a calamity already known. In both cases the Day has reached the face before it has finished arriving.

## Living it

The passage draws a straight line from a habit of the heart to a face on the Day of Judgement, and it is worth taking that line seriously.

**The diagnosis in ayah 20 is not about scholarship.** Ibn Kathir's point is that rejection of the Hereafter grows out of preoccupation with the present life and distraction from what comes after. Very few of us would say we disbelieve in the Last Day; the question the ayah actually asks is narrower and harder — is it *left*? "Neglect," in ayah 21, is not a verdict a person announces. It is what happens to something you never get round to.

**The Prophet ﷺ attached a practical instruction to this very promise.** When he ﷺ told the Companions that they would see their Lord as they see the full moon, he added in the same breath: if you are able to avoid missing a prayer before the rising of the sun — Fajr — or before its setting — ʿAsr — then do so. The narration does not spell out why those two prayers are named alongside that promise. It simply puts the promise and the instruction in one sentence, and leaves us to keep them together.

**And the highest reward turns out to be the simplest thing.** In the narration Muslim alone records, the people of Paradise have already been saved from the Fire, already had their faces whitened, already been admitted to the Garden — and when Allah offers them something extra, what they receive is nothing they had thought to ask for, and nothing given to them was more beloved to them than it: looking at their Lord. If that is the summit, then the love named in ayah 20 is not merely a bad investment. It is a smaller love, accepted in place of the greatest one on offer.

passages.title: The soul at the collarbone: the moment of death
passages.tafsir:
# The soul at the collarbone: the moment of death

These five ayat are a single scene, and both commentaries read them as one. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes all five together in one block and then says simply that the verse *depicts the scene of death*. Ibn Kathir moves through them in a single run — quoting ayah 26 together with ayah 27 as one statement, then the entwined shanks, then the closing line — without breaking the scene into separate lessons. So this reading follows the scene rather than dividing it: a soul rising to the collarbones, a room casting about for anyone who can help, a dying person who now knows this is the parting, legs entwined and no longer his to move — and one last line naming where all of it is going: **to your Lord**.

## Where the passage sits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out what has just been said. The preceding verses described the reckoning on the Day of Reckoning and the conditions of the inmates of Paradise and of Hell. Now man's attention is drawn from that far horizon to something much nearer: **his own approaching death**, which he should not neglect. And the reason is stated plainly — he should embrace the faith and do deeds of righteousness *before* death overtakes him, so that he may attain salvation in the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir opens his comments on the passage with a single sentence of theme — Allah informs of the condition at the time of death and what terrors it contains — and then, before explaining a single word of it, he prays: *May Allah make us firm at that time with the Firm Statement.* The prayer comes first, ahead of the commentary. That is a good indication of how he expected these ayat to be read. They are not a report about other people.

## "Kallā" — the word that stops you

The passage opens with **كَلَّا** (*kallā*), rendered here as "But no!" and in Ibn Kathir's translation as "Nay". Ibn Kathir gives two ways of taking it, and both are worth carrying.

- Taken as a **negation**, the meaning is: *O son of Adam! You are not able to deny that which I informed you of at that time* — that is, at death. His reason follows: "This will become something witnessed by you with your own eyes." Denial ends where sight begins.
- Taken as a **word of affirmation** — and Ibn Kathir says that on this reading "this would be the most obvious meaning" — it carries the sense *it is certainly true*: it is certainly true that when the soul reaches the collarbones… Here the word is not shutting down a denial; it is underlining a fact.

## The soul at the collarbones, and a room that cannot help

**التَّرَاقِي** (*al-tarāqī*) are the collarbones — the clavicles, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders them. Ibn Kathir spells out what is meant, and notice whom he says it to: *your soul will be pulled out of your body and it will reach your collarbones.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the same moment inside a life: the unmindful man forgets his death until his soul comes up to his collarbone.

Ibn Kathir places this beside a similar statement of Allah (56:83–87), where the soul reaches the throat:

> "Then why do you not (intervene) when (the soul of the dying person) reaches the throat? And you at the moment are looking on, but We are nearer to him than you, but you see not, then why do you not, if you are exempt from the reckoning and recompense, bring back the soul, if you are truthful?"

That is a demand no one at the bedside can meet. The people in the room are *looking on* — present and powerless. And the ayah says something staggering about that instant: Allah is nearer to him than they are, though they do not see it. The room may be crowded and useless; the dying man is not unattended.

Then the room speaks. **وَقِيلَ مَنْ رَاقٍ** — "And it will be said: 'Who can cure him?'" The word *rāq* is read two ways in the sources:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**, reported by ʿIkrimah: "who is the person who recites divine prayers of healing so that he may come and cure him?" — that is, someone to perform *ruqyah*, healing recitation.
- **Abu Qilābah**: "who is the doctor that can cure him?" — and Ibn Kathir notes that **Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd** all have similar statements.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds both together in one line and catches the escalation exactly: the healers fail to heal him, and the people look for enchanters to save him. This is the moment medicine hands the case over and the family starts reaching for anything at all. The question goes up into the room — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has already told us the outcome the room will not admit. The healers fail.

## He knows it is the parting, and the shanks are entwined

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the next two lines into one motion, and it is worth following its wording closely: *when one shank is entwined with the other, he realizes that it is the final moments of his parting.* The physical fact and the inner recognition arrive together. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the same line is "And he will think that it was the parting"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses it as his realising that it is the time of departure from the world.

And then comes the sentence that turns this scene into a personal emergency for the reader: **at this juncture neither is his repentance acceptable nor a righteous deed.** The certainty arrives precisely when it can no longer be used. Hence the conclusion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws: it is necessary for a wise person to make amends *before* this moment arrives.

**وَالْتَفَّتِ السَّاقُ بِالسَّاقِ** — "and one shank is intertwined with the other shank." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *sāq* means "shank", the lower leg. This is the most discussed image in the passage, and the commentaries lay several readings side by side without ruling between them.

**The physical readings.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two: that being agitated and restless, he strikes one shank on the other, or rubs one against the other; or that if one leg is placed on the other and the dying person wants to move it, he would not be able to do so — and it notes that **ash-Shaʿbī and al-Ḥasan** have interpreted it in this second way. Ibn Kathir reports **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** saying, "These are your two shins when they are bound together," and in another narration from him a line that lands like a blow: *his two legs have died and they will not carry him while he used to walk around on them.* The legs that carried him everywhere are done carrying him. (The translation carried here renders the image as the feet being tied together in a shroud — a rendering in the same physical register.)

**The two worlds meeting.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reports from **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "This is the last day of the days of this world and the first day of the days of the Hereafter. So there will be hardships that will meet more hardships, **except for he whom Allah has mercy upon.**" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the same view from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the two shanks refer to the two worlds, the Here and the Hereafter: one affliction joined to another, the agony of leaving this world joined to the agony of the punishment awaiting the disbeliever in the next.

That exception clause is where light enters the passage, and it is not a small opening. The hardship is described as general; the escape is described as mercy.

**ʿIkrimah** said: the great matter joined with the great matter. **Mujāhid** said: a test joined with a test. Whichever layer you hold, the sense is compounding — one hardship meeting another.

## To your Lord

**إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ** — "The drive will be on that Day to your Lord." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: on that day, it is to your Lord that one has to be driven. Ibn Kathir glosses *al-masāq* as **the place of return and the destination**.

Note who the destination is. Not the grave, not the Hereafter in the abstract, but **your Lord** — the same one who, in the passage Ibn Kathir quoted a moment earlier, is nearer to the dying man than the people standing over him.

Ibn Kathir then describes what happens: the soul ascends into the heavens, and Allah says, *"Return my servant to the earth, for verily, I have created them from it, I return them into it, and from it I will bring them out at another time."* He notes that this has been reported in the lengthy Hadith of al-Barāʾ. Death, on this account, is not an ending but a turn in a course Allah has already set in three stages — created from the earth, returned into it, brought out of it again at another time. We affirm this as it has come, without asking how.

He anchors the scene in one more statement of Allah (6:61–62):

> "He is the Irresistible (Supreme), over His servants, and He sends guardians over you, until when death approaches one of you, Our messengers take his soul, and they never neglect their duty. Then they are returned to Allah, their True Master. Surely, for Him is the judgement, and He is the swiftest in taking account."

Read alongside the closing line of our passage, that fills in what the dying person cannot see. Guardians have been sent. The messengers who take the soul never neglect their duty. And the handover to Allah is immediate — He is "the swiftest in taking account."

## Living it

The passage is short on comfort and long on urgency, and the practical conclusion is drawn for us, so it is worth stating without decoration.

**Do now what you are counting on doing later.** Faith, repentance, righteous deeds — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that at this juncture neither repentance nor a righteous deed is accepted, and that a wise person therefore makes amends before the moment arrives. The window these ayat describe is not narrow; by the time the scene begins, it is closed.

**Read it in the second person.** It would be easy to watch this scene from the doorway — *he* realises, *his* legs, *who can cure him.* Both commentators refuse that vantage point. Ibn Kathir's own gloss addresses the reader directly — *O son of Adam*, *your soul*, *your collarbones* — and his very first response to the passage is to pray for firmness at that hour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the man in the scene simply "the unmindful man", which is to say: whoever is not thinking about this.

May Allah make us firm at that time with the Firm Statement, and place us among those whom He has mercy upon on the day this world's last day meets the first day of the next.

passages.title: The denier who neither believed nor prayed
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about**

These five ayat are a verdict passed on a life — delivered immediately after the Qur'an has shown us that life's final minutes. In the ayat just before (26–30), a dying man's soul rises to his collarbones, the people around him cast about for anyone who might save him ("Who can cure him?" — 'Ikrimah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this means looking for someone who recites prayers of healing, while Abu Qilabah said it means looking for a doctor, and Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said much the same), and he understands that this is the parting. Of "one shank will be joined with another shank" (ayah 29), the early authorities differed: Ibn 'Abbas took it as the last day of this world meeting the first day of the Hereafter, "hardships that will meet (more) hardships, except for he whom Allah has mercy upon"; 'Ikrimah as "the great matter (will be joined) with the great matter"; Mujahid as "a test (will be joined) with a test"; and Al-Hasan Al-Basri as the two shins bound together — in another narration from him, "His two legs have died and they will not carry him while he used to walk around on them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a similar reading from Sha'bi and Hasan: the dying man wants to move one leg off the other and cannot. And, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "at this juncture neither is his repentance acceptable nor a righteous deed."

Ayat 31–35 then turn the camera around and show *why* that deathbed looked like that. Ayat 31–33 give a whole biography in four verbs and one gesture; ayat 34–35 pronounce the verdict on it, said twice over. That is what holds the passage together: a life described, then sentenced.

## Ayat 31–32: a whole life in four verbs

> "This denier neither believed nor prayed, but persisted in denial and turned away."

The Arabic lays the four verbs out in a deliberate pattern. Ayah 31 says what he did *not* do: *ṣaddaqa* — to affirm something as true — and *ṣallā* — to pray. Ayah 32 then supplies the exact opposite of each, in the same order: *kadhdhaba*, he declared it false, and *tawallā*, he turned away. The connector at the head of ayah 32 is *wa-lākin*, which Ibn Kathir renders "but, on the contrary" — the ayah is not restating an absence, it is naming its opposite.

Ibn Kathir reads the pairing precisely. These ayat, he says, "inform about the disbeliever who used to deny the truth in his heart in the abode of this worldly life, and he used to turn away from acting according to its way." So in his reading the first verb belongs to the heart and the second to the limbs: he would not accept the message inwardly; he would not bend to it outwardly. Ibn Kathir's conclusion is stark: "there is no good in him, internally or externally."

That is a two-sided ledger, and prayer is what stands on the outward side of it. Belief and ṣalāh are named together, and both are missing.

## Ayah 33: the walk home

> "then went to their own people, walking boastfully."

The verb is *yatamaṭṭā*. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of Ad-Dahhak, glossed it in one word: "arrogantly." Qatadah and Zayd bin Aslam both said: "Strutting." Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "he walked in conceit (full pride) to his family admiring himself," and, summing up ayat 31–33 together, names the character behind the walk — "stubborn, cruel, obstinate, wanton, lazy, having no concern and doing no deeds."
