Watch the sequence: *thumma dhahaba*, "then he went." He has just met the truth and pushed it away — and the very next thing he does is walk home to his own people, pleased with himself. Ibn Kathir links this to two other scenes in the Qur'an. Of the mockers of the believers: "And when they returned to their own people, they would return jesting" (83:31). And of another such man: "Verily, he was among his people in joy! Verily, he thought that he would never come back (to Us)!" (84:13–14) — on the last words of which Ibn Kathir comments simply, "meaning, return."

So the strut is not a small vanity. It belongs to a man who supposed there would be no coming back. And the ayah Ibn Kathir quotes next is the answer to that supposition: "Yes! Verily, his Lord has been ever beholding him!" (84:15). He was being seen the whole time — walking home, admiring himself, sure nobody was watching.

## Ayat 34–35: the fourfold woe

> "Woe to you, and more woe! Again, woe to you, and even more woe!"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *awlā* is the inverted form of *wayl*, and *wayl* means destruction. It then explains why the word appears four times across these two ayat: destruction is heaped four times on the man who "has made it his habit to deny and reject" and died in that state — at the time of death, in the grave, at the time of Resurrection, and finally at the time of entering Hell. Four woes for four moments.

Ibn Kathir calls the two ayat "a definite warning and threat from Allah to those who disbelieve in Him and strut about when walking," and he catches the tone exactly. The sense, he says, is: *you deserve to strut like this while you have disbelieved in your Creator and Maker* — "this is what is commonly said in this type of situation in order to mock and intimidate."

That is a recognisable Qur'anic register, and Ibn Kathir gathers its parallels: "Taste you (this)! Verily you were (pretending to be) the mighty, the generous!" (44:49); "Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little. Verily, you are criminals" (77:46); "So worship what you like besides Him" (39:15); "Do what you will" (41:40). In every one of them, the words appear to grant permission while what is actually being announced is doom. Ayat 34–35 do the same to the strut of ayah 33: *go on, walk like that.*

## The moment behind the words

There is a specific occasion behind this wording, and it makes the passage vivid.

Abu 'Abdur-Rahman An-Nasa'i recorded from Sa'id bin Jubayr that he raised these two ayat with Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Abbas replied: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said this to Abu Jahl, then Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, revealed this Ayah."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a fuller version from Qatadah — who transmits the incident with a note of caution, "They claim" — that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ grabbed the clothes of Abu Jahl and said to him, "Woe to you! And then (again) woe to you! Again woe to you! And then (again) woe to you!" Abu Jahl's answer was this: "Are you threatening me, O Muhammad? By Allah! Neither you nor your Lord are able to do anything, and verily, I am the mightiest person walking between its (Makkah's) two mountains."

Read that reply back against ayah 33 and the passage locks together. Abu Jahl's boast is itself a boast about *walking* — the mightiest man who walks between Makkah's two mountains. Here is a man who has just heard the truth from the Prophet ﷺ face to face, denies it, turns away, and measures himself against the two mountains of his own city. And on Ibn 'Abbas's account, ayat 34–35 are the Prophet's ﷺ words to him made permanent revelation. Qatadah's own summary of the two ayat is as plain as it gets: "It is a threat followed by a threat, just as you hear it."

Abu Jahl is the occasion, not the limit. Ibn Kathir reads the warning as directed at all "those who disbelieve in Him and strut about when walking" — the description is a type, and the ayat were preserved for everyone who fits it. (The sūrah then presses on, in ayah 36, to the assumption underneath the strut: "Does man think that he will be left neglected?" — which belongs to the passage after this one.)

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical point of this whole section: man's attention is being drawn to his approaching death, "which he should not neglect. He should embrace the faith and do deeds of righteousness before death overtakes him, so that he may attain salvation in the Hereafter... Therefore, it is necessary for a wise person to make amends before this moment arrives."

Three things this passage asks concretely:

**Check both halves, not one.** Ayat 31–32 audit the heart and the limbs together, and Ibn Kathir's phrase — "no good in him, internally or externally" — is a two-column ledger. Belief and prayer are named side by side because, on this reading, they belong side by side: the inward assent and the outward act.

**Watch the walk home.** The most searching image here is ayah 33: how a person leaves an encounter with the truth. Does he go back to his own circle lighter, more self-satisfied, quietly pleased that he brushed the demand off? That is the gesture the fourfold woe is answering. And per 84:15, that walk is seen.

**Do it now, because the door in ayat 26–30 closes.** The four points Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists — death, the grave, the Resurrection, the entry into Hell — are all still ahead. The only place in that sequence where anything can still be changed is the one we are standing in, before the soul reaches the collarbones. After that, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, neither repentance nor a righteous deed is accepted.

And Allah knows best.

passages.title: From a drop to a person: proof of resurrection
passages.tafsir:
Sūrat al-Qiyāmah closes the way a case closes — with the argument that settles it. After the scene at the deathbed, and after the portrait of the man who "neither believed nor prayed" but denied, turned away, and walked home admiring himself, Allah puts a single question to that man about his own body — and then answers it by telling him where that body came from. These five ayat are one continuous proof: ayah 36 puts the question, ayat 37–39 lay out the evidence, and ayah 40 draws the conclusion. Three of the five are questions. The listener is not being lectured; he is being cross-examined.

## Who is being asked

Ayah 36 speaks about "man," and the man in view has just been described. Ibn Kathir, commenting on the ayat immediately before, says they inform us about "the disbeliever who used to deny the truth in his heart in the abode of this worldly life, and he used to turn away from acting according to its way. Thus, there is no good in him, internally or externally." Of his walk home — "Then he walked in conceit to his family admiring himself" — Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means "arrogantly," and Qatadah and Zayd bin Aslam both said, "Strutting."

That is the man whom ayah 36 stops in his tracks with a question.

## Ayah 36: "left neglected" — and the two things that means

The Arabic word at the heart of ayah 36 is **sudā** — rendered "left without purpose," or, in Ibn Kathir's translation, "left neglected." The early authorities read it in two ways, and Ibn Kathir records both.

**As-Suddi** said it means "not resurrected" — does man imagine that death is simply the end of him, that he goes into the ground and nothing follows?

**Mujahid, Ash-Shafi'i and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam** all said it means "he will not be commanded and prohibited" — does man imagine he was put here with no law over him, nothing required of him, nothing forbidden to him, free to do as he pleases with no one to answer?

Ibn Kathir does not choose between them. "Apparently the Ayah includes both meanings," he writes, and then joins them into a single sentence: man "will not be left neglected in this worldly life, without being commanded and prohibited. He also will not be left neglected in his grave unattended to without being resurrected. Rather he will be commanded and prohibited in this life, and gathered back to Allah in the abode of the Hereafter."

That joining is the heart of the ayah. On Ibn Kathir's reading the two meanings are not rivals but two ends of one rope: a life under command, and a day on which that life is gathered back to Allah. Neglect would have meant neither — no law now, no reckoning later. The ayah denies both.

Ibn Kathir states the purpose of the passage plainly: "The intent here is to affirm the existence of the abode of the final return and to refute whoever rejects it from the people of deviance, ignorance and stubbornness."

## Ayat 37–39: the evidence, stage by stage

Having put the question, the Qur'an does not answer it with a threat. It answers with a fact the listener cannot dispute, because it happened to him. "Thus," writes Ibn Kathir, "Allah uses the beginning of creation as a proof for the repetition of the creation."

**Ayah 37 — the drop.** "Was he not a *Nutfah* of semen emitted?" A *nuṭfah* is a drop of fluid. Ibn Kathir's gloss holds nothing back: "was not man a weak drop of sperm from a despised fluid known as semen, that is emitted from the loins into the wombs?" Three words in one line, and every one of them is lowly — *weak*, *despised*, *emitted*. Whatever the man in ayah 33 has to strut about, this is the address the question sends him back to.

**Ayah 38 — the clot, and the shaping.** "Then he became an *'Alaqah*; then shaped and fashioned in due proportion." An *ʿalaqah* is a clinging clot. Ibn Kathir traces the sequence that follows: "he became a clot, then a lump of flesh, then he was formed and the soul was blown into him. Then he became a perfect creation with healthy limbs." Note what the ayah says was done and does not say who did it — until Ibn Kathir supplies the answer in the next breath: all of it "by the permission and decree of Allah."

**Ayah 39 — two out of one.** "And made of him two sexes, male and female." From one drop come two whole kinds of human being — "either a male or a female," Ibn Kathir says, "by the permission and decree of Allah."

Set out as Ibn Kathir sets it out, the evidence climbs a staircase: despised fluid → clinging clot → lump of flesh → a formed body → the soul breathed in → a perfect creation with healthy limbs → male or female. Not one of those steps was arranged by the man they produced.

## Ayah 40: the conclusion

"Is such a One unable to bring the dead back to life?"

The ayah does not name Allah here; it points — "*such* a Creator," the One the listener has just watched at work through three ayat. Ibn Kathir unpacks exactly what is being pointed at: "is not He Who made this perfect creation from this weak drop of sperm able to repeat that as He did originally?"

That is why the proof needs no premise the denier does not already grant. He is not asked to accept an unseen report. He is asked to look at the harder thing — a whole person assembled out of a drop of fluid — which has already happened, to him, and then to say with a straight face that the easier thing, restoring a body that has already existed once, is beyond the One who did it the first time.

**Where the scholars differed.** Ibn Kathir notes a genuine difference over what Allah's power "to repeat that" covers: on one view it refers to the origination only — bringing the person back into existence; on the other it covers both that and the process of perfecting him. He connects the question to Allah's words, "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; this is easier for Him" (30:27). His own comment is a model of scholarly restraint: "The first view is more popular, and Allah knows best."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** puts the same conclusion as a plain appeal to reason: "Can it be imagined that the Supreme Being in whose controlling power is death and life and the entire world is not able to bring the dead to life?"

## From the Sunnah: answer the question out loud

The surah ends on a question — and the Sunnah teaches the reciter to answer it.

**Abu Dawud** recorded from Musa bin Abi 'A'ishah that a man used to pray on top of his house, and whenever he recited "Is it not so then, that He would be able to give life to the dead?" he would say, **"Glory to You, of course."** When the people asked him about it he said, "I heard it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Ibn Kathir is candid about the report's standing: Abu Dawud was alone in transmitting this hadith, and he did not mention who this Companion was — "but there is no harm in that."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** records the practice in slightly fuller words, reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever recites this verse of Sūrat al-Qiyāmah should say: بلی وانا علی ذالک من الشھدین — "Yes indeed, I am among those who bear witness that He has the power to do it." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not name the collection this comes through, so it is passed on here as the teaching it conveys and not attributed to any named book.) The same report attaches responses to two parallel questions elsewhere in the Qur'an: at "Is Allah not the Greatest Ruler of all the rulers?" (95:8) the reciter says the same words, and at "Now, in which discourse, after this, will they believe?" (77:50) he says, "I believe in Allah."

There is something quietly beautiful in this. Allah closes the surah by putting a question to man; the Prophet ﷺ taught man not to let the question hang in the air. The denier of ayah 36 heard a question about himself and walked on. The believer hears it and says *balā* — *yes indeed* — and in saying it he steps out of the category the surah has been describing.

## Living it

**Being commanded is not a burden but a dignity.** Read ayah 36 the way Mujahid and Ash-Shafi'i read it: the alternative to being told what to do is being *left neglected*. Every obligation on a believer — prayer, fasting, honesty, restraint — is a sign that Allah did not leave him lying about like something forgotten. The next time an obligation feels heavy, consider what its absence would actually mean.

**Remember the drop.** The Qur'an sets these ayat side by side: the man walking home admiring himself, and then, a line later, the weak drop from a despised fluid that he once was. Whatever a person has by way of wealth, position or strength was handed to a creature who began the way ayah 37 describes. That is a cure for arrogance available to anyone willing to keep the two pictures in view at once.

**Answer the ayah when you reach it.** Whether in the prayer or in private reading, when you come to ayah 40, do not read past it — answer it, in the words reported from the Prophet ﷺ. It takes a second, and it turns a passage about someone else's denial into your own testimony.
